sections.learningObjectives:
- Recognize common specimen rejection criteria, including hemolyzed, mislabeled, unlabeled, clotted, and wrong-container specimens, and explain why each is rejected.
- Document specimen collection, patient identification, collection issues, refusals, and corrections accurately and in accordance with office policy.
- Report specimen problems and collection issues to the appropriate staff through the established chain of command.
- Escalate patient-safety concerns, exposure incidents, and unclear situations to licensed staff or supervisors rather than acting beyond scope of practice.
- Apply standard precautions and bloodborne pathogen safety practices when handling, transporting, and disposing of specimens, including rejected ones.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

It is like a lunchbox with the wrong name tag: you cannot just guess whose lunch it is, so you need a new, correctly labeled one.

### Question 2

Before handing someone their papers, you check two things about them, like their name and birthday, so you know it is really them.

### Question 3

It is like writing a child's name on their cup right as you pour the drink, so no one's cup gets mixed up with a friend's.

### Question 4

Hemolysis is when the red blood cells break open, like a red balloon popping in clear water and turning the water pink.

### Question 5

If you shake a juice bottle really hard, it froths and changes; shaking a blood tube too hard breaks the red cells inside.

### Question 6

If you write the wrong name on a birthday gift tag, you do not scribble it out — you start over with a clean tag.

### Question 7

A paper with no name on it cannot be turned in for credit — no one knows whose work it is.

### Question 8

If a recipe needs a special ingredient to work, using the wrong ingredient means you have to start the recipe over.

### Question 9

QNS is like not having enough juice in the cup to run the taste test — you need a fuller cup.

### Question 10

It is like a smoothie that was supposed to stay liquid but turned lumpy — it is no longer right for the recipe.

### Question 11

Documenting is like signing and dating your homework so the teacher knows when and by whom it was done.

### Question 12

It is like writing down which two clues you used to make sure you gave the right package to the right person.

### Question 13

Treat every tube like it might have germs you cannot see, and always wear your gloves — just like wearing a raincoat even when the sky looks clear.

### Question 14

If you get a splinter, you wash it and tell a grown-up right away — you do not keep playing and hope it is fine.

### Question 15

When you are not sure about a rule, you ask the teacher instead of guessing — the teacher knows the right answer.

### Question 16

You cannot just switch a name tag to fix a mix-up — you have to redo the label the right way.

### Question 17

Using an expired tube is like baking with spoiled ingredients — the result cannot be trusted.

### Question 18

If a friend says no to something, you do not force them — you write down that they said no and tell the person in charge.

### Question 19

Before mailing a letter, you double-check that the name on the envelope matches the letter inside.

### Question 20

It is like fixing a mistake in a notebook by crossing it out neatly and writing the right answer next to it, so everyone can still see what happened.

### Question 21

If you see a spill in the hallway, you tell a grown-up right away so nobody slips.

### Question 22

A contaminated culture is like a dirty sample in a science project — you start over with a clean one to get a true answer.

### Question 23

It is like explaining the rules of a game before playing, so everyone does it the right way the first time.

### Question 24

Before you start, you check the instructions match the assignment so you do the right thing for the right person.

### Question 25

It is like pouring the plain juice before the fancy syrup so the syrup does not change the flavor of the next cup.

### Question 26

Red blood cells are like tiny bags of salt (potassium); when the bags pop, the salt spills into the liquid and the test reads too high.

### Question 27

Leaving a rubber band around a finger too long changes the finger; leaving the tourniquet too long changes the blood sample.

### Question 28

It is like a recipe that needs exactly one spoon of mix for one cup of water — if the amounts are off, the recipe fails.

### Question 29

Lipemia is like adding cream to coffee until it turns cloudy and light.

### Question 30

If a test is supposed to happen at 9:00 but happens at 11:00, the results do not mean the same thing, so you must tell the teacher.

### Question 31

If water is running through one hose, you would not sample from that same hose and expect pure water — you would use a different hose.

### Question 32

A fresh sample is like fresh food — leave it out too long and it changes and cannot be trusted.

### Question 33

Some things must stay cold, like ice cream — leave them out and they melt and are ruined.

### Question 34

If it took you two tries to do something, you write that down so the next person knows it was tricky.

### Question 35

Writing down where you took the sample is like noting which arm you used, so everyone knows the details later.

### Question 36

In a digital notebook, you add a correction note instead of secretly erasing, so there is a record of what changed and why.

### Question 37

It is like writing down the batch number on a box of supplies so you can find them if something goes wrong.

### Question 38

If the science project did not have enough liquid to test, you gather more and try again — you do not pretend it worked.

### Question 39

If a photo comes out blurry, you kindly ask to take it again instead of blaming the person or making up a story.

### Question 40

If a friend starts to feel faint during a game, you stop, make sure they are safe, and call for a grown-up.

### Question 41

Sharp things go straight into a special strong box, like putting broken glass in a safe bin instead of the regular trash.

### Question 42

After you tell a grown-up about a cut, they may still check it and decide if you need more help — telling is the first step, not the last.

### Question 43

A spill is cleaned up safely with gloves and the right cleaner, like cleaning up a mess with the right supplies instead of your bare hands.

### Question 44

When you have a problem at school, you tell your teacher, who tells the principal if needed — you follow the chain.

### Question 45

The assistant is like the person who delivers the report card but the teacher explains what the grades mean.

### Question 46

If you are unsure about a rule, you ask before acting — like checking the instructions instead of guessing.

### Question 47

Writing down what happened and why, like a note to the teacher, so everyone knows the assignment was not finished and why.

### Question 48

Before putting a name tag on something, you check the name against two reliable clues to be sure it is right.

### Question 49

If you are supposed to catch the middle of the stream and you do not, you start over the right way instead of pretending it is fine.

### Question 50

If you are collecting every raindrop for a day and miss one, the total is wrong, so you start over.

### Question 51

If a test needs an empty stomach and the person just ate, you tell the teacher before starting, because the answer would be wrong.

### Question 52

A culture is like planting seeds — too few seeds may mean nothing grows even when it should.

### Question 53

A cracked cup of juice is thrown away and the drink is poured again — you do not tape the crack and hope.

### Question 54

Like letting hand sanitizer dry before you touch things, you let the cleaning wipe dry so it works properly.

### Question 55

If you almost trip on a loose rug, you tell someone so it gets fixed before anyone actually falls.

### Question 56

If frozen food thaws and you refreeze it, it is not the same; you tell the person in charge it thawed.

### Question 57

Serum comes from blood that has clotted; plasma comes from blood kept liquid with a special ingredient.

### Question 58

If you forgot a special step in a recipe, you tell someone and redo it instead of serving the wrong result.

### Question 59

A STAT test is like an urgent message that must be delivered right away, not left in a pile.

### Question 60

It is like stamping the time on a package so you know it arrived fresh and on time.

### Question 61

If the washing machine makes a scary noise, you stop it and tell a grown-up instead of letting it run.

### Question 62

To get a clean sample, you handle it gently instead of shaking it hard.

### Question 63

You kindly say the sample could not be used and ask to try again, without pointing fingers.

### Question 64

Writing down the instructions you gave is like leaving a note so the next helper knows what you already explained.

### Question 65

If two clues do not match, you stop and figure out the mix-up before going any further.

### Question 66

Even a broken or rejected sample still might have germs, so you keep wearing gloves when handling it.

### Question 67

The wrong name is a stop-and-redo problem, while the other choices are all things done the right way.

### Question 68

Fixing the wrong name on a test is more important than neatening a smudge, because the wrong name could hurt someone.

### Question 69

Red, milky, or yellowish samples are like colored water that can trick the measuring machine, so the lab has to be careful.

### Question 70

Even if you are pretty sure whose cup it is, you do not guess when the label is missing — you get a new, properly labeled one.

### Question 71

If a recipe needs exactly one cup of water for one spoon of mix, adding too much water ruins the recipe.

### Question 72

A medicine level is like checking how much is in the body at a certain time after a pill; checking at the wrong time gives a confusing answer.

### Question 73

If the measuring cup had a leak, you would not trust the amount it showed — you would point out the leak first.

### Question 74

Wash it, tell a grown-up right away, and then do the follow-up the grown-up says — in that order.

### Question 75

For something important, you keep a signed list of everyone who touched it, like tracking a special package at every step.

### Question 76

Do not copy an old note and paste it without checking, because old mistakes would follow into the new note.

### Question 77

If an assignment is rejected, you write down why and what to do next so it gets finished properly.

### Question 78

Tell the person in charge about the mistake so it can be fixed the right way.

### Question 79

A culture is like taking a clean sample of pond water — if you scoop up mud too, the answer is muddled, so you sample again carefully.

### Question 80

A wrong name on a test cannot be fixed on paper — you redo the test with the right name.

### Question 81

You can never fake a name tag to fix a mix-up — you always start over the honest way.

### Question 82

If you do not stir the sugar into the tea quickly, it clumps; a blood tube must be mixed right away so it does not clot.

### Question 83

Label each cup right when you pour it, one person at a time, so no two cups get mixed up.

### Question 84

If the same mistake keeps happening, you look for the reason and fix the rule, not just shrug and repeat it.

### Question 85

The assistant is like a lookout who calls for the lifeguard when they see a problem — they do not try to rescue alone.
